analysis.one_liner: Guts federal endangered species protections and hands states power over species within their borders.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and died in committee when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the Endangered Species Act so that federal agencies could not list a species without the consent of every governor whose state it lives in, and Congress could not protect a species without voting to approve it by name. Any species found in only one state could be taken over entirely by its governor, with no court able to review that decision, and every species would automatically come off the protected list after five years unless Congress re- approved it. It would also let landowners proceed with projects that harm protected habitat if a federal agency misses a 90-day reply deadline, pay landowners 150% of their property's value when a wildlife ruling blocks a use, and cut off reimbursement of lawyer fees for citizens who sue to enforce the law.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners and lessees of large landholdings — developers, timber, mining, oil and gas, and agricultural operators — gain the most. A governor's veto over listings, a 90-day silence rule that deems projects approved, 150% compensation for any ruling that cuts a property's intended-use value by half, and a five-year sunset on every listing all remove the main federal check on building, logging, drilling, or plowing habitat where endangered or threatened species live. Energy customers would see federal endangered-species compliance costs itemized on their power bills, a framing designed to build opposition to the law. Ranchers gain an exception allowing them to kill black vultures threatening livestock, and states gain authority over ravens that prey on recovering species.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large landowners, developers, timber and extractive industries

how_it_helps.text: A species could not be federally listed without the consent of the governor of every state where it is present, and lists could not take effect until Congress enacted a joint resolution approving them by name.

Governors could claim exclusive authority over any endangered or threatened species found only within their state — writing rules, permits, critical habitat, and recovery plans — and their actions would be exempt from judicial review in any federal or state court.
Every federally listed species would automatically come off the protected list five years after approval unless Congress passed a new resolution to relist it.

Landowners could get a written ruling on whether a project violates the law, and if the Interior Department failed to answer within 90 days the project would be deemed legal and shielded as an affirmative defense to any penalty or prosecution.
If a wildlife ruling diminished a property's fair market value by 50% or more for its intended use, taxpayers would have to pay the owner or lessee 150% of that value within 180 days.

Citizens who sue to enforce the Endangered Species Act would no longer recover attorney fees, removing the main way ordinary people and conservation groups can afford to go to court over wildlife enforcement.

Four federal power administrations would have to bill customers monthly for their share of endangered-species compliance costs, including foregone power generation, making the act's costs visible on household and business power bills.

analysis.who_pays: Everyone who relies on functioning ecosystems and public lands bears the cost of weakened species protection: rare plants and animals found in a single unfriendly state would effectively lose federal protection, and five-year automatic delisting would repeatedly strip protection from species still recovering. Taxpayers would fund 150% payouts to landowners. Rivers and public lands where species recoveries depend on reduced power generation would face renewed pressure. The bill's findings also declare that endangered-species listings are a tool to undermine infrastructure, signaling a policy of clearing regulatory hurdles for construction.
analysis.who_pays_short: Imperiled wildlife, taxpayers, and public lands users

drawbacks.text: The bill responds to a real burden: the Endangered Species Act can restrict how private land is used with no payment, which the bill's own findings call a penalty on landowners who happen to own habitat, and compensation and fast determinations would address that grievance.

Requiring Congress to vote on each species list and re-approve every listing every five years would make protection hostage to legislative calendars and lobbying, and automatic delisting would repeatedly strip protection from species still recovering.

Exempting a governor's species decisions from all judicial review, while removing attorney fees for citizens who sue, would leave no practical way to challenge state mismanagement or force federal enforcement.
The 90-day deemed-approval rule invites agencies to miss deadlines and rewards applicants who wait out a slow federal office, potentially legalizing habitat destruction by default.
Paying 150% of fair market value for unfavorable rulings would turn wildlife protection into a taxpayer-funded liability far above actual property loss.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There are genuine grievances here — landowners do bear real costs when habitat rules limit their property, and the bill's compensation idea, however generous, is an honest response to that. But the price of this particular fix is enormous: a governor veto over listings, congressional approval for each species, automatic five-year delisting, no judicial review of state decisions, and no lawyer-fee recovery for citizen enforcers would together hollow out the Endangered Species Act, while taxpayers would owe landowners 150% payouts. The bill offered no offsetting benefit to the public at large.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Natural Resources Committee and a wildlife subcommittee from October 2021 until the Congress ended in January 2023, never getting a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Perry introduced the bill on October 12, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
Two days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water, Oceans, and Wildlife, which was the last action the bill ever received.
No other member joined as a cosponsor, so the bill entered committee with no visible support in the House.
The committee never scheduled a markup or hearing, no version was ever voted on, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Endangered Species Act's existing protections remain intact, and the landowners, developers, and extractive interests the bill would have benefited got nothing. Because the bill died without a vote or cosponsors, no one invested in it gained anything.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, and no votes were ever taken, so no party breakdown exists.

industries.industry: Real estate developers and large landowners
industries.note: Governor veto power over listings, deemed-approval after 90 days, and 150% taxpayer compensation would remove the main federal check on developing habitat. The public bears the cost as weakened species protection and compensation payouts.

industries.industry: Timber, mining, and oil and gas operators
industries.note: Automatic five-year delisting and state takeover of intrastate species would clear endangered-species hurdles to logging, mining, and drilling on public and private land.

The bill lets ranchers kill black vultures threatening livestock or property and lets states control ravens that prey on recovering species, addressing real predation losses while easing habitat restrictions on farmland.

The bill does not change compliance requirements but would itemize endangered-species costs, including foregone power generation, on monthly bills from four federal power administrations — a transparency step that is also built to turn ratepayers against the law.
Eliminating attorney-fee awards in endangered-species citizen suits removes the funding mechanism that makes private enforcement of wildlife law possible.
